claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a confirmed single-phase solid solution with high baseline toughness.
Service-level mechanical loading causes the single-phase matrix to develop localized segregation and precipitation at grain boundaries.
Dislocation accumulation and local compositional fluctuations under high stress and elevated temperature cause the precipitates to form.
The resulting precipitates are brittle structural mediators.
The precipitates cause a marked loss of toughness and promote brittle fracture.
Mechanical loading introduces dislocation pile-ups and strain gradients.
Dislocation pile-ups and strain gradients trigger localized compositional fluctuations.
Localized compositional fluctuations promote nucleation of brittle precipitates at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
The precipitates compromise the integrity of the homogeneous solid solution.
Compromising the homogeneous solid solution reduces toughness and favors brittle rather than ductile failure.
Loaded specimens will exhibit localized precipitation or segregation detectable by TEM or atom-probe tomography.
Loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness than the pristine baseline.
Loaded specimens will initiate cracks earlier than the pristine baseline.
The proposed behavior applies under high strain rates and/or elevated temperatures representative of demanding aerospace or automotive service.
Under low-stress or room-temperature conditions, the single-phase structure should remain stable.

contradictions.description: The intervention makes elevated temperature part of the loading condition, whereas the boundary states that high strain rate and elevated temperature may each be sufficient. The additional assertion that room-temperature environments should remain stable conflicts with the possibility, implied by the stated 'and/or' boundary, that high-strain-rate loading alone could trigger the behavior at room temperature.
